n: Jesus stays in Galilee for a while because the leaders in Judea are now plotting to kill him. In John, “the Jews” usually means the hostile religious authorities, not the Jewish people as a whole.

f.g: Jewry = Judea, the southern region around Jerusalem.

n: The autumn Feast of Tabernacles is approaching — a joyful week-long festival when families lived in leafy booths to remember Israel’s wilderness journey.

f.g: Also called Sukkot or the Feast of Booths; one of three pilgrimage feasts to Jerusalem.

n: Jesus’s brothers urge him to go to Judea and show his miracles where they will be noticed, so his followers there can see them.

f.g: Younger brothers in Mary’s family: James, Joses, Simon, and Judas.

n: Their reasoning sounds practical — nobody who wants fame works in secret — but it reveals they see his mission as a bid for public popularity.

f.g: shew = show. Compare Satan’s similar challenge to display power in Matthew 4:5-6.

n: John explains that even Jesus’s own brothers did not yet believe in him. Later, after the Resurrection, they would become believers and leaders.

f.w: neither did his brethren believe in him

n: Jesus answers that his timing is set by his Father’s plan; theirs is not, so any time suits them.

f.w: My time is not yet come

f.g: alway = always.

n: The world has no reason to hate them, since they fit in; it hates Jesus because he exposes its evil deeds.
He tells them to go on to the feast without him; he isn’t going up yet, because his appointed time hasn’t fully arrived.

f.g: Many manuscripts read “I go not up,” but the sense is that he would not go publicly with them on their terms.

n: So Jesus remains in Galilee for the moment.

f.g: abode = stayed, remained.

n: After his brothers leave, Jesus goes up quietly, without a public procession. He goes on God’s timetable, not as a show.

f.g: Privately, avoiding the crowds of pilgrims on the road.

n: At the festival the authorities are looking for him and keep asking where he is.

f.g: Their question shows he is already the talk of Jerusalem.

n: The crowds whisper and argue: some call him a good man, others a deceiver leading people astray.

f.g: Here, low-voiced debate and gossip among the crowds.

n: Yet no one dares speak openly about him because they fear the religious leaders.
Halfway through the week-long feast, Jesus appears in the temple courts and begins teaching publicly.

f.g: About the fourth day of the eight-day festival.

n: The leaders are amazed that he knows the scriptures so well without having studied under a recognized rabbi.

f.g: letters = learning, especially formal training in the scriptures.

n: Jesus explains that his teaching isn’t his own invention; it comes from the Father who sent him. His authority is divine, not academic.
Here is a key promise: anyone willing to live God’s will can come to know for themselves whether Jesus’s teaching is from God. Obedience opens the door to testimony.

f.w: If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine

n: A self-promoter seeks his own glory; one who seeks to glorify the one who sent him can be trusted. Jesus points glory to the Father.
Jesus turns the tables: Moses gave them the law, yet they don’t keep it — and plotting murder breaks it outright.

f.w: Why go ye about to kill me?

n: The crowd, unaware of their leaders’ plot, accuse him of being possessed or paranoid.

f.g: An insult meaning “you’re crazy” or “a demon is speaking through you.”

n: Jesus refers to the one miracle that caused so much uproar on his last visit — healing the paralyzed man at Bethesda on the Sabbath.
He points out that they circumcise baby boys even on the Sabbath when the eighth day falls then — a practice that goes back to the patriarchs, before Moses.

f.g: From Abraham and the patriarchs, long before the law of Moses.

n: If they will perform a ritual on one part of the body on the Sabbath to keep the law, why be angry at him for making a whole person well on the Sabbath?

f.g: every whit = completely, in every part.

n: Stop judging by surface appearances, he urges; judge fairly and righteously.
Some Jerusalem residents, who know about the plot, wonder aloud whether this is the man the leaders want to kill.

f.g: Local residents, as opposed to the pilgrims visiting for the feast.

n: They are puzzled that he speaks boldly and no one stops him. Could the rulers have secretly concluded he is the Messiah?

f.g: Christ = Greek for “Anointed One,” the same meaning as the Hebrew “Messiah.”

n: They dismiss the idea: they know where he’s from, while popular belief held that the Messiah would appear from an unknown origin.

f.w: no man knoweth whence he is
f.g: A popular belief that the Messiah would be hidden until suddenly revealed.

n: Jesus calls out in the temple: they know his earthly hometown, but not his true origin. He has been sent by the Father — whom they do not truly know.
Jesus, by contrast, knows the Father personally because he comes from him and was sent by him.
They try to arrest him, but no one can lay a hand on him, because his “hour” — the time of his suffering and death — has not yet come.

f.w: his hour was not yet come

n: Meanwhile many ordinary people believe, reasoning that the Messiah could hardly do more miracles than this man.

f.w: many of the people believed on him

n: Hearing this support grow, the Pharisees and chief priests send temple police to arrest him.

f.g: Temple guards under the authority of the chief priests.
The high priest and leading members of the priestly families, mostly Sadducees.

n: Jesus says he will be with them only a little longer before returning to the Father who sent him.

f.w: Yet a little while am I with you

n: They will look for him and not find him, because they cannot follow where he is going — into the presence of God.

f.w: where I am, thither ye cannot come
f.g: thither = there, to that place.

n: His hearers misunderstand, guessing he will go teach Jews scattered abroad or even Gentiles. Ironically, his gospel would soon go to the Gentiles.

f.g: The Diaspora — Jews living outside the land of Israel.

n: They puzzle over his words but don’t grasp them.

f.w: What manner of saying is this
f.g: What kind of statement is this?

n: On the final, greatest day of the feast — when priests poured water at the altar praying for rain — Jesus stands and cries out: anyone who is thirsty should come to him and drink.

f.w: If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink
f.g: During the feast a priest drew water from the Pool of Siloam and poured it at the altar each morning.

n: Whoever believes in him will become a source of “living water” — life flowing out to others, as the prophets foresaw.

f.g: belly = the innermost being, the heart.

n: John explains that the living water is the Holy Ghost, whom believers would receive after Jesus was glorified through his death and resurrection.

f.w: the Holy Ghost was not yet given
f.g: The JST reads that the Holy Ghost “was promised unto them who believe, after that Jesus was glorified.”

n: Some listeners now conclude that Jesus is “the Prophet” whom Moses foretold.
Others declare he is the Messiah. But skeptics object that the Messiah could not come from Galilee.

f.w: Shall Christ come out of Galilee?

n: They cite scripture: the Messiah is to be David’s descendant from Bethlehem. Ironically, Jesus was both — they simply didn’t know his story.
The crowd splits into factions over him. Jesus often divides people because he requires a decision.
Some want to seize him, yet no one actually does.

f.w: no man laid hands on him

n: The temple officers return empty-handed, and the leaders demand to know why.

f.w: Why have ye not brought him?

n: The officers’ answer is a remarkable testimony from unlikely witnesses: no one has ever spoken the way this man speaks.

f.w: Never man spake like this man

n: The Pharisees sneer: have the officers been fooled too?

f.g: led astray.

n: They argue from authority: none of the rulers or Pharisees believe — as if truth depended on the approval of the elite.

f.g: Members of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council in Jerusalem.

n: They dismiss the common people as ignorant of the law and therefore cursed — a contemptuous attitude Jesus repeatedly rejected.

f.w: this people who knoweth not the law

n: Nicodemus, himself a member of the council who once came to Jesus by night, speaks up.
He reminds them that their own law forbids condemning a person without first hearing him and learning the facts. Quietly, Nicodemus is beginning to stand for Jesus.

f.w: Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him

n: They mock him as a Galilean sympathizer and claim no prophet comes from Galilee — overlooking that Jonah was from Gath-hepher in Galilee.

f.w: out of Galilee ariseth no prophet

n: The meeting breaks up and everyone goes home, the question about Jesus still unresolved.

f.w: every man went unto his own house
f.g: Many ancient manuscripts lack the passage from here through John 8:11, though it is widely regarded as a genuine story about Jesus.
